titleText.es: Tristemente, esto es una historia real. Al menos aprendí el comando 'say' de OS X.
titleText.en: Sadly, this is a true story.  At least I learned about the OS X 'say' command.

applications.explanationEn: Puedo changes poder for the speaker, while preguntar stays in its unchanged -ar form as the action for which permission is requested.

regions.labelEs: NO PUEDO ENTRAR, ESTOY INTENTANDO QUE MI COMPAÑERA DE PISO ME ABRA.

applications.explanationEn: Puedo is the form of poder for the speaker, and entrar remains in its unchanged -ar form as the possible action.
Estoy matches the speaker, and intentando uses -ando to present the attempt as currently in progress.

applications.exampleEs: INTENTANDO QUE MI COMPAÑERA DE PISO ME ABRA
applications.explanationEn: Intentando names the attempt, que introduces the different actor mi compañera de piso, me identifies who benefits, and ordinary abre changes to the attempted-action form abra.
Compañera takes the feminine form for the person, while de piso completes the conventional expression for a shared-apartment roommate.

regions.labelEs: PRIMERO INTENTÉ LLAMARLA AL MÓVIL, PERO LO TIENE APAGADO.

applications.explanationEn: Intenté changes for the speaker in completed past time, while llamar stays in its unchanged -ar form before the attached la.
La is attached to the unchanged verb llamar to represent the female person receiving the call.
Lo replaces the masculine phone and stands directly before the changed verb form tiene.
Lo replaces the masculine phone, tiene presents its maintained state, and apagado describes that state with a matching masculine ending.

regions.labelEs: LUEGO LO INTENTÉ POR EL IRC, PERO NO ESTÁ CONECTADA.

excludedUnits.rationale: IRC is an English technical initialism for Internet Relay Chat, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Lo replaces the previously described attempt and stands directly before the changed past verb form intenté.
Está presents the current result, while conectada is conectar's completed form with a feminine ending matching the woman already under discussion.

regions.labelEs: NO HE ENCONTRADO NADA PARA TIRARLE A LA VENTANA,

applications.explanationEn: He is the helper for the speaker, and encontrado is encontrar's completed-action form.
No stays before the completed verb phrase because nada follows it; both negatives reinforce one negative meaning in Spanish.
Para introduces the intended purpose, and tirarle stays in its unchanged -ar form with le attached.
Le attaches to the unchanged verb tirar and marks the person affected by what happens to the item named afterward.
Here the attached le points to the female roommate as the person affected.
Because le has already identified the female roommate, la introduces the feminine item associated with her.
The le attached to tirar identifies the affected owner, while la agrees with the feminine item ventana; natural English expresses that relationship with a possessive.

regions.labelEs: ASÍ QUE ME CONECTÉ POR SSH AL MAC MINI DEL SALÓN Y USÉ EL SINTETIZADOR DE VOZ PARA DECÍRSELO.

excludedUnits.rationale: SSH is an English technical initialism for Secure Shell, not a Spanish lexical word.
Mac Mini is an unchanged Apple product name rather than Spanish curriculum vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Así and que form the result connector that introduces the next action as a consequence.
Para introduces the purpose, and decir stays in its unchanged form inside decírselo.
Se and lo attach to the end of decir, and the written accent preserves the verb's stress.
Inside decírselo, se represents the recipient and comes before lo, which represents the thing being told.
He is the present helper for the speaker, and quedado is quedar's completed-action form.
Me marks quedarse for the speaker, he quedado places the result in completed time, and fuera names the outside state interpreted here as being locked out.

regions.labelEs: PERO CREO QUE DEJÉ EL VOLUMEN MUY BAJO, ASÍ QUE ME ESTOY LEYENDO LA DOCUMENTACIÓN DE OS X PARA AVERIGUAR CÓMO SUBIR EL VOLUMEN POR LÍNEA DE COMANDOS.

excludedUnits.rationale: OS X is an unchanged operating-system product name rather than Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Dejé names the completed action, el volumen fills the affected-object slot, and muy bajo states the low level left in place.
Así and que combine to introduce the next action as a result.
Estoy matches the speaker, and leyendo uses -iendo to present the reading as in progress.
Me adds the sense of working through the specified reading, while estoy leyendo supplies the matching ongoing form.
Para introduces the purpose, and averiguar stays in its unchanged -ar form.
Cómo keeps its written accent because it asks for the unknown method, and subir follows in its unchanged -ir form.

applications.exampleEs: CÓMO SUBIR EL VOLUMEN POR LÍNEA DE COMANDOS
applications.explanationEn: Cómo introduces the unknown method inside a larger statement, so it keeps its written accent even without question marks around this clause.
Subir supplies the increase action, and el volumen names the sound level being raised.
Línea names the text interface, and de comandos specifies that it accepts computer commands.

regions.labelEs: ENTIENDO QUE EL TIMBRE NO FUNCIONA.

cards.noteEn: Puedo is the form of poder for the speaker. In a question, it can ask whether an action is allowed rather than whether the speaker is capable of doing it.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

cards.noteEn: Intentando is the -ando form of intentar. It presents the attempt as an action in progress or happening alongside another description.

example.en: He keeps trying to open the door.

cards.promptEs: intentar que + otra persona + acción en subjuntivo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone tries to get another person to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of intentar, then que, name the other person when needed, and put that person's action in its special non-factual form.
cards.noteEn: That special form is called the subjunctive. It presents the later action as the goal of the attempt rather than an established fact: ordinary abre changes to abra, and ordinary viene changes to venga. If the same person both tries and acts, use intentar followed directly by the action verb in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form instead.

example.en: We try to get Pablo to arrive early.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: female roommate; female flatmate (in compañera de piso)
cards.noteEn: Compañera can mean a female companion or colleague. With de piso, it conventionally names a female person who shares the same apartment.

example.es: Mi compañera de piso cocina muy bien.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “roommate” or “flatmate”?
cards.answerEn: Use compañero de piso for a man and compañera de piso for a woman.
cards.noteEn: Compañero or compañera names the person sharing something, and de piso specifies the shared apartment. Make compañero or compañera match the person's gender; piso stays unchanged.

example.es: Mi compañero de piso trabaja de noche.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’
Piso can mean a floor or storey. In Spain it also commonly means an apartment or flat where someone lives.

cards.answerEn: opens; lets someone in (special form for an attempted or desired action)
cards.noteEn: Abra is a special form of abrir used when the opening is being attempted, wanted, allowed, or otherwise not stated as a fact. Compare ordinary ella abre, “she opens,” with intento que ella abra, “I try to get her to open.”

example.es: Espero que Luis abra la puerta.
example.en: I hope Luis opens the door.

cards.noteEn: Primero can describe the first step in an order. In a question about preparation, it can mean “first” or “beforehand.”
Intenté is the completed-past form of intentar for the speaker.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone tries to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of intentar followed directly by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: No linking preposition is needed between the two verbs. Intento abrir means “I try to open,” and intentamos salir means “we try to leave.” The attempted action stays in its basic -ar, -er, or -ir form.

example.en: We try to open the window.

cards.answerEn: to call her; to phone her
cards.noteEn: Llamar is the unchanged dictionary form meaning “to call,” and la is attached to its end for a female person receiving the call.

example.en: I am going to call her this afternoon.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.answerEn: on the; a + el before the phone being called
cards.noteEn: Al combines a and el. With llamar, Spanish can use it before the phone or number where a person is being contacted; natural English often says “on.”

example.en: I called him on his cell phone.

cards.noteEn: Móvil is the ordinary word for a cell phone in Spain. Many Latin American regions instead use celular.

example.es: Mi móvil está en la mochila.
example.en: My cell phone is in the backpack.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.

cards.promptEs: tener + objeto + participio que describe su estado
cards.questionEn: How do you say that you have a person or thing in an assigned, prepared, closed, or other resulting state?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tener, name or replace the object, and add its completed-action form as a description.
cards.noteEn: The completed-action form is often called a past participle. Here it behaves like a describing word and matches the object: tengo la puerta cerrada, but tengo los documentos preparados. This differs from haber plus a participle, where the participle does not change.
Apagado describes a masculine singular device that is not operating. The ending changes to apagada for a feminine singular thing.
Por can identify the channel used to communicate: por teléfono, por radio, or por videollamada. Natural English often uses ‘on,’ ‘by,’ or ‘over’ rather than translating por with one fixed word.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; article before a masculine technical name
cards.noteEn: Spanish can keep el before the name of a masculine service, protocol, or technical system even when English uses the name by itself.

cards.promptEs: estar + forma de acción completada que describe un estado
cards.questionEn: How do you describe the state something is in as the result of an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by the action's completed form, with an ending that matches the thing being described.
cards.noteEn: The completed form, often ending in -ado or -ido, is also called a participle. Estar changes for who or what is in the state. The participle changes like a describing word: cerrado, cerrada, cerrados, or cerradas. This pattern focuses on the resulting state, not on who performed the action.
Conectada describes a female person or feminine thing that has a network connection. The -a ending matches that feminine referent.

cards.questionEn: Why can a Spanish sentence contain both no and another negative word?
cards.answerEn: When the second negative word follows the verb, keep no before the verb too.
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses matching negative words together. No tiene ninguna means “it does not have any”; it does not become a positive meaning as two negatives sometimes do in formal English.

example.en: I do not have any doubt.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.answerEn: to throw something at someone's property; le marks the affected owner
cards.noteEn: Tirar is the unchanged action form, and le attaches to its end for the person affected. Spanish can then use an ordinary article before that person's item, where natural English often uses “her” or “his.”

example.es: A Ana le tiraron pintura a la puerta.
example.en: Someone threw paint at Ana's door.

cards.promptEs: me arreglan el móvil · van a lavarle el coche
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish identify the person affected through a body part, possession, or other closely connected noun without putting a possessive word before it?
cards.answerEn: Mark the affected person with me, te, le, nos, or les, then use el, la, los, or las before the closely connected noun.
cards.noteEn: The short person word goes before a changed verb, as in le repararon, or attaches to an unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form, as in repararle. The article matches the related noun, whether it names a body part, possession, service, or closely associated aspect. Natural English often expresses that relationship with my, your, his, her, our, or their.

example.es: Van a lavarle el coche a Ana.
example.en: They are going to wash Ana's car.

cards.answerEn: at; toward (introducing what something is thrown at)
cards.noteEn: After tirar or tirarle, a can introduce the person or thing used as the target.

example.es: Tiraron una pelota a la pared.
example.en: They threw a ball at the wall.

cards.answerEn: the; English often uses a possessive because le already marks the affected owner
cards.noteEn: Spanish can use le for the affected owner and an ordinary article before that person's item. La matches a feminine singular item, not the owner's gender; natural English often uses “her” or “his” instead.

example.es: Le cerraron la cuenta a Marta.

cards.answerEn: so; therefore (as part of así que)

cards.questionEn: How do you connect a situation to its result with “so”?
cards.answerEn: Use así que before the result.
cards.noteEn: Así que joins a cause or situation to what follows from it. The two words work together as one connector; translating así and que separately will not give the intended meaning.

example.es: Está lloviendo, así que llevo un paraguas.
example.en: It is raining, so I am carrying an umbrella.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a result connector
no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.
With me before it, conecté is the completed-past form of conectarse for the speaker: me conecté means “I connected” or “I logged in.”

cards.promptEs: OS X · say · sintetizador de voz por línea de comandos
cards.questionEn: What makes it possible for a Mac to speak text from the command line?
cards.answerEn: OS X includes a command named say that sends typed text to the system speech synthesizer.
cards.noteEn: A terminal command is text entered into a command-line interface. Running say followed by words makes the Mac read those words aloud; command-line tools can also adjust settings such as volume. The joke depends on remote access to the Mac and this built-in speech tool.
Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.

cards.answerEn: in the; de + el identifying something by its location
cards.noteEn: Del combines de and el. After an object, it can identify which one by naming the room or place associated with it, where natural English often says “in” or puts the location before the object name.

example.en: We use the table on the patio.

cards.noteEn: Usé is the completed-past form of usar for the speaker. The written accent distinguishes this past form from the special present form use.
A sintetizador de voz is a speech synthesizer: software or hardware that produces spoken audio.

example.es: El sintetizador produce una voz artificial.
example.en: The synthesizer produces an artificial voice.

cards.noteEn: Decir is the unchanged action form. In this sense, se stands for “to her,” and lo stands for the thing told. Both attach to the end, and the written accent keeps the original stress. In another context, se could instead refer to him, formal you, or them.

example.en: I have to tell it to her tomorrow.

cards.promptEs: le/les + lo/la/los/las → se lo/se la/se los/se las
cards.answerEn: Use se for the recipient, followed by lo, la, los, or las for the thing.
cards.noteEn: Le or les normally means “to him,” “to her,” “to you” (formal), or “to them.” Immediately before lo, la, los, or las, it changes to se; Spanish does not say le lo. Se still stands for the recipient, while the second word stands for the thing. Le doy el libro a Ana therefore becomes se lo doy.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “I give it to her/him/them” without repeating the person and the thing?

example.es: Le doy el libro a Ana. → Se lo doy.
example.en: I give the book to Ana. → I give it to her.

cards.noteEn: Oye is the informal singular command form of oír, “to hear.” In conversation it commonly gets one person's attention, like “hey” or “listen.”

example.en: Hey, I need to talk to you.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is locked out or left outside?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of quedarse followed by fuera.
cards.noteEn: Quedarse describes ending up or remaining in a state, and fuera means outside. Context can make quedarse fuera mean being unable to enter, or “being locked out,” rather than merely choosing to stay outdoors. Match me, te, se, nos, os, or se and the form of quedar to the person and time.

example.es: Olvidé las llaves y me quedé fuera.
example.en: I forgot the keys and was locked out.

cards.answerEn: ended up; remained (completed form of quedarse)
cards.noteEn: Quedado is used with a form of haber to place quedarse in a completed time. A following word can name the resulting state or place.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone leaves or causes a thing to remain in a certain state?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of dejar, name or replace the affected thing, then add the words that describe its resulting state.
cards.noteEn: Dejar changes for the person and time. The object is the person or thing affected, and the final description tells the state it remains in. If that description is an adjective, it matches the object: dejé la puerta abierta but dejé los cajones abiertos.
Here bajo is a describing word for a masculine singular level or setting. It is different from bajo meaning “under” and from bajo meaning “I lower.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; presents the reading as working through a specified text
cards.noteEn: With leer, me can add the sense that the speaker works through the stated text. It does not mean the speaker reads themself. The same completion pattern uses te, se, nos, os, or se for other people.

example.en: I read through the report last night.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish emphasize reading, eating, or drinking a whole, clearly specified thing?
cards.answerEn: Choose me, te, se, nos, os, or se to match the person doing the action, and use it with the reading, eating, or drinking verb.
cards.noteEn: These small words can present the action as carried through over the complete book, meal, drink, or stated amount; they do not mean that the person acts on themselves. Compare leer un libro, “read a book,” with leerse un libro, which often suggests reading it through. The small word normally goes before a verb form that shows person and time, as in se leyó; it attaches to an unchanged dictionary form, as in leerse. This completion nuance is not required every time.

example.es: Ana se leyó la novela en dos días.
example.en: Ana read through the novel in two days.

cards.noteEn: Leyendo is leer in its ongoing-action form ending in -iendo.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what, how, or where to do something without naming a new person who does it?
cards.answerEn: Use an accented question word, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. This compact pattern is used when the person who would perform the action is already clear from context. The question word keeps its written accent even inside a larger statement: qué hacer, cómo llegar, dónde aparcar.

example.en: I do not know where to park.

cards.questionEn: When “what,” “how,” or “where” introduces unknown information inside a larger sentence, does Spanish keep the written accent?
cards.answerEn: Yes. Keep the accent in qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo, cuál, or quién even when the question is embedded inside a statement.
cards.noteEn: An embedded, or indirect, question reports what is unknown rather than asking it as a separate sentence. It may have no question marks, but the question word still carries its accent. Compare no sé dónde vive, “I don't know where she lives,” with the relative form donde in la casa donde vive, “the house where she lives.”

example.en: I don't know where she lives.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “turn the volume up”?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of subir followed by el volumen.
cards.noteEn: Subir can mean that something goes up or that someone raises it. With el volumen as its object, it conventionally means increasing the sound level. Change subir for the person and time; el volumen stays the same.

example.en: Can you turn the volume up?

cards.answerEn: through; along; down; via (a movement path)
cards.noteEn: Por can mark the path followed during movement. English may choose through, along, down, or via according to the route.

cards.answerEn: line; part of línea de comandos (“command line”)
cards.noteEn: In computing, línea de comandos names a text interface where a person types instructions for the computer.

example.es: Escribo la orden en la línea de comandos.
example.en: I type the instruction on the command line.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “command line”?
cards.noteEn: This is the conventional computing term for a text interface where a person types commands instead of choosing controls in a graphical interface. Línea stays singular, while comandos is normally plural.

example.es: Abro el programa desde la línea de comandos.
example.en: I open the program from the command line.

cards.noteEn: Ah can show that the speaker has just understood, noticed, or recognized something. Its exact English equivalent depends on tone.

cards.answerEn: I take it; I gather; I understand (an inference)
cards.noteEn: Entiendo que can introduce a conclusion drawn from what has just been said, much like English “I take it that...” It need not mean that the speaker has received an explanation.

example.en: I take it you are not coming today.
